name: The 100-word world
do: One exactly-100-word fragment per session, all set in one fantasy world: a place, a creature, a rumor, a scene. No plot planning.
tests: Whether worldbuilding alone pulls you, apart from the pressure of a finished story.

name: One poem a week, revised daily
do: Draft a short poem on Monday, then spend each later session revising only that poem. New poem the next Monday.
tests: Whether you enjoy the craft of revision, which is most of sustained writing.

name: Letters to your kid
do: One short philosophical letter per session to your future child: what a good life is, what you fear, what marriage taught you.
tests: Whether writing tied to your real life outlasts writing about invented worlds.

name: The serialized story
do: Write a story in installments of about 300 words. Stop mid-sentence every time so the next session has an obvious start.
tests: Whether momentum and an audience of one keep you returning.
source: Hemingway's stop-while-going-good rule, serial fiction hooks

name: Philosophical fieldnotes
do: Carry a pocket notebook. Each session, take one observation from ordinary life and develop it into a paragraph-long argument or question.
tests: Whether a portable, observation-driven practice fits your life better than desk-bound writing.

name: Object writing
do: Ten minutes, one object, all seven senses (sight, sound, taste, touch, smell, organic, kinesthetic). No complete sentences required.
tests: Whether sensory drilling feeds everything else you write.

name: Evening page
do: One paragraph on the day, then one principle you hold tested against what actually happened.
tests: Whether philosophy as a daily practice beats philosophy as essays.

name: Thirty questions of worldbuilding
do: Answer one structured worldbuilding prompt per session: geography, religion, trade, law, food, death rites.
tests: Whether systematic building or improvised fragments is your mode.

name: Golden shovel
do: Take a line you love and use its words, in order, as the last word of each line of a new poem.
tests: Whether borrowed structure removes blank-page friction.
source: Terrance Hayes form, The Daily Poet

name: Erasure
do: Black out a photocopied page of philosophy you have read until a poem remains.
tests: Whether playing with other people's text lowers the bar to start.

name: Dialogue only
do: 200-word scenes in pure dialogue between two characters in your world. No narration.
tests: Whether voice is where your energy lives.

name: One aphorism
do: Write one aphorism, then in later sessions cut it until nothing is spare.
tests: Whether compression is the craft you enjoy.

name: The house in twenty rooms
do: A short vignette for each room, corner, and view in the new house.
tests: Whether present life is better material than invented life.

name: Trip postcards
do: On trips, one postcard-length piece a day about where you are and who you are with.
tests: Whether travel is fuel instead of a gap.

name: Retell a myth
do: Retell a known myth or fairy tale in 500 words with one rule changed.
tests: Whether a borrowed plot frees you from planning.

name: Read one, write one
do: Read one poem, then write a response poem in 15 minutes.
tests: Whether input is what you have been missing.

name: The strongest objection
do: Pick one philosophical position you hold. Each session, write the best case against it.
tests: Whether dialectic pulls you more than exposition.

name: Microfiction for your wife
do: One text-message-sized story sent to your wife every day.
tests: Whether an audience of one sustains you.

name: A character a day
do: One character sketch per session for your world, no plot, until a cast exists.
tests: Whether people or places draw you into fantasy.

name: Voice memo drafts
do: Dictate a paragraph on a walk or commute. Polish it in the evening.
tests: Whether speaking unblocks you.

name: One tune, three weeks
do: Pick one standard at your level. Head, comping voicings, a simple solo, then play it in a second key.
tests: Whether depth on one tune is more rewarding than broad coverage.
source: Open Studio's pathway works one tune every six weeks

name: The 15-minute Open Studio slice
do: One Open Studio course that matches your level (Level 3 or Jazz Piano Expansions). 15 minutes per session, pick up exactly where you stopped.
tests: Whether structured learning gives more progress per minute than self-directed practice.
source: Open Studio Level 3, Jazz Piano Expansions

name: Transcribe four bars
do: Transcribe and learn four bars of a solo you love, by ear, every session.
tests: Whether ear-driven learning is what actually excites you.

name: Record every session
do: Normal practice, then a one-minute recording at the end. Never delete any. Compare first and last at trial end.
tests: Whether audible proof of progress changes motivation.

name: Compose a lullaby
do: Write a simple original piece for the baby using the harmony you are learning. One phrase or chord change per session.
tests: Whether composing at the piano pulls you more than playing standards.

name: Guided practice with the trio
do: One Open Studio Guided Practice Session per sitting, nothing else.
tests: Whether playing with a band track is the hook.

name: ii-V-I around the clock
do: One rootless voicing type (A or B) through all 12 keys, one key per session.
tests: Whether drilling satisfies or drains you.

name: Learn a tune by ear only
do: Listen five to ten times, sing the melody, then find it at the piano. No lead sheet.
tests: Whether ear-first learning sticks better.

name: Comping study
do: Eight bars of Wynton Kelly comping behind a soloist. Rhythm placement first, then voicings. Play along.
tests: Whether accompaniment pulls you more than soloing.

name: Left hand only
do: Walking bass or stride under a simple melody, ten minutes.
tests: Whether a narrow technical focus is satisfying.

name: iReal Pro, chart hidden
do: One standard with iReal Pro backing, chart hidden. Five bpm faster each session.
tests: Whether tempo and memory challenges motivate you.

name: Sixth-diminished scale
do: Barry Harris's major sixth diminished scale in one key per session, then harmonize a melody with it.
tests: Whether a harmony system grabs you.

name: Blues in twelve keys
do: One key per session: head plus two choruses.
tests: Whether blues form is a home base.

name: Reharm a song she loves
do: A pop tune or hymn your wife likes, one chord substitution per session.
tests: Whether reharmonization is your creative outlet.

name: Trade fours with yourself
do: Record a four-bar phrase, answer it, repeat.
tests: Whether call and response unlocks improvisation.

name: Ballad only
do: One slow tune for three weeks. Voicings and touch.
tests: Whether beauty rather than chops pulls you.

name: Block chords, one slice
do: One lesson from Block Chords Made Easy applied to a melody each session.
tests: Whether a sound-specific goal keeps you returning.

name: Five minutes before bed
do: No agenda. Play one tune freely for five minutes.
tests: The smallest possible floor. Newborn-season default.

name: Friday for your wife
do: A two-minute performance of the week's work for your wife every Friday.
tests: Whether a weekly audience closes the loop.

name: Sing it first
do: Sing a four-bar phrase over a backing track, then find it on the keys.
tests: Whether the ear-to-hands link is your gap.

name: The ugly-beat sprint
do: One finished 60-second track per session or two. Finished, not good. Bounce it, name it, move on.
tests: Whether finishing tiny things removes the intimidation.

name: Piano into the box
do: Record a voicing or short line from your piano practice and build a track around it.
tests: Whether production feels yours when it starts at the piano.

name: One-track deep dive
do: Rebuild four to eight bars of a song you love: just the drums, or just the bass and chords.
tests: Whether imitation is less intimidating than a blank project.

name: Three-sound constraint
do: Every track uses only three sounds or instruments.
tests: Whether small palettes make production playful.

name: Words on beats
do: Set your own poems or prose to music, as spoken word over a beat or sung lyrics.
tests: Whether combining two interests is more life-giving than keeping them apart.

name: One synth for everything
do: One virtual instrument for every sound, drums included.
tests: Whether a single instrument beats a plugin folder.

name: Sample your house
do: Phone-record household sounds, build a drum kit, make a beat.
tests: Whether found sound is your way in.

name: Ninety-second flip
do: Same sample every session, a new 90-second piece each time.
tests: Whether constraints on source material speed you up.
source: Ableton and Andrew Huang Start Here challenge

name: Drum drills
do: One genre's drum pattern in ten minutes. New genre each session.
tests: Whether rhythm is your fast lane.

name: Eight bars a day
do: One loop, bounced, never arranged.
tests: Whether arrangement is the intimidating part.

name: Arrange the pile
do: Take old loops and turn one into a two-minute arrangement each session.
tests: The opposite of eight bars a day: whether arranging is the fun part.

name: Reference skeleton
do: Mark a favorite song's structure with markers, then fill each section with your own parts.
tests: Whether borrowed structure removes paralysis.

name: Delete the drums
do: Take a sketch, remove a major element, rebuild around the hole.
tests: Whether destruction unlocks decisions.

name: No presets
do: Design one sound from an initialized patch per session. Save it to a personal bank.
tests: Whether sound design is the life-giving part.

name: Ten tracks max
do: Every project capped at ten tracks.
tests: Whether a ceiling speeds finishing.

name: Score a scene
do: Sixty seconds of music for a movie clip or a photo from a trip.
tests: Whether a picture gives you direction.

name: Produce for a mood
do: One mood for the whole trial, such as nursery at 3 a.m.
tests: Whether an emotional brief beats a technical one.

name: A genre a week
do: Three weeks, three unfamiliar genres.
tests: Whether novelty or depth motivates you.

name: Mix only
do: No new notes. Sessions spent only mixing one sketch against a reference.
tests: Whether mixing is the scary part.

name: Phone-only production
do: Sketch in a phone app on trips, import later.
tests: Whether removing the desk removes the dread.
